source_text: Quotienscumque, fratres mei, causam istam Maximianistarum, quam sicut potui uobis exposui, eis cum in collatione ageremus obiecimus, plus inde tacuit quam modo in omnibus tacet. non se occultent tergiuersatoria non defensione sed fuga. dicunt enim, quod dilationem illis dederint et intra dilationem illos susceperint. hoc falsum est; duodecim cum Maximiano damnati sunt, ceteri autem non aderant ordinationi eius, quando ei manus imposita est. illis dilationem dederunt; nam uerba ipsius ista sunt: nec solum hunc, inquit, sceleris sui mors iusta condemnat; trahit etiam ad consortium criminis plurimos catena sacrilegii, de quibus scriptum est: (uenenum aspidum sub labiis eorum quorum os maledictione et amaritudine plenum est. ueloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem. contritio et infelicitas in uiis eorum, et uiam pacis non cognouerunt. non est timor dei ante oculos eorum\'. nollemus quidem tamquam proprii corporis secare iuncturam.sed quoniam tabescentis uulneris putredo pestifera plus habet in abscisione solaminis quam in remissione medicaminis, inuenta est causa salubrior, ne per cuncta membra pestilens irreperet uirus, ut compendioso dolore natum decidat uulnus. famosi ergo criminis reos esse nominat duodecim, inter quos et Felicianum et Praetextatum, sed nomina omnium mihi non occurrunt; et sic infert: qui funesto opere perditionis uas sordidum collecta faeculentia sordidarunt, sed et clericos aliquando ecclesiae Carthaginis, qui, dum facinori intersunt, illicito incestui praebuerunt lenocinium, dei praesidentis arbitrio uniuersalis concilii ore ueridico damnatos esse cognoscite. eos autem, quos sacrilegi surculi non polluere plantaria, hoc est qui a Maximiani capite proprias manus uerecundo fidei pudore retraxerunt, ad matrem ecclesiam redire permisimus. uolebant pumicare faciem suam, quia sacrilegis ignoscebant et aperte schismaticis uiam redeundi concedebant. quid est hoc, rogo. modo mihi dignetur exponere, quomodo eos sacrilegi surculi non polluere plantaria. quare illis dilationem das, si nullam partem in Maximiani schismate habere potuerunt? si autem socii sunt factionis, quamuis non fuerint praesentes ordinationi, quomodo illos non inquinat Maximianus, et totum orbem terrarum semel absens damnatus, tertio praesens absolutus inquinat Caecilianus? non inquinat Afer Afros, uiuus uiuos, notus notos, particeps socios, et Caecilianus inquinat transmarinos, inquinat longe positos, (inquinat ignotos,) inquinat nondum natos? tecum sedit a te damnatus, et non te inquinauit Felicianus? ego illum non uidi, tu illum nosti; ego illum innocentem credo, tu istum nocentem damnasti. aut si fateris innocentis te fuisse receptorem, fateris te innocentis fuisse damnatorem.
thought_title: The Maximianist case exposes Donatist inconsistency
orientation: Augustine is addressing the congregation in the Catholic church, pressing the Donatist bishop Emeritus on the Maximianist schism that the Donatists themselves condemned and then received back.
pass_a_gloss: As often as, my brothers, this case of the Maximianists, which as I was able to you I have explained, to them when in conference we were conducting we objected, more about it he was silent than now in all things he is silent. Let them not hide themselves [with] evasive not [with] defense but [with] flight. They say indeed, that a delay to them they gave and within the delay them they received. This false is; twelve with Maximian were condemned, the rest however not were present [at] the ordination of him, when to him hands were imposed. To them a delay they gave; for the words of him these are: not only this one, he says, of his crime death just condemns; it draws also to [the] partnership of [the] crime many [by] the chain of sacrilege, about whom it is written: (the poison of asps under the lips of them whose mouth with cursing and bitterness full is. Swift [are] the feet of them to [the] shedding of blood. Crushing and unhappiness in the ways of them, and [the] way of peace not they have known. Not is [the] fear of God before the eyes of them). We would not wish indeed as of [our] own body to cut [the] joint. But since of [the] wasting wound the putrefaction pestilential more has in [the] cutting of relief than in [the] application of medicine, was found a cause more salutary, lest through all [the] members [the] pestilent should creep virus, so that with brief pain [the] grown [thing] should cut off [the] wound. Of infamous therefore crime [the] guilty to be he names twelve, among whom both Felicianus and Praetextatus, but [the] names of all to me not occur; and thus he brings in: who by [the] deadly work of perdition [the] vessel filthy [with] collected filth they defiled, but also [the] clerics at some time of [the] church of Carthage, who, while in [the] crime they are present, to [the] illicit incest they offered [the] pimping, by [the] of God presiding judgment [the] of [the] universal council [with] mouth truth-speaking [to have been] condemned know. Those however, whom of [the] sacrilegious shoot not did pollute [the] plantings, that is who from [the] Maximian head [their] own hands [with] shamefaced of faith [with] modesty drew back, to [the] mother church to return we permitted. They were wishing to pumice [the] face of them, because to [the] sacrilegious they were pardoning and openly to [the] schismatics [the] way of returning they were granting. What is this, I ask. Now to me let him deign to explain, how them of [the] sacrilegious shoot not did pollute [the] plantings. Why to them a delay do you give, if no part in [the] Maximian schism to have they were able? If however [the] allies they are of [the] faction, although not they were present [at] [the] ordination, how them not does pollute Maximianus, and [the] whole [the] circle of lands once absent condemned, [the] third time present absolved does pollute Caecilianus? Not does pollute [the] African [the] Africans, [the] living [the] living, [the] known [the] known, [the] sharer [the] allies, and Caecilianus does pollute [the] overseas, does pollute [the] far placed, (does pollute [the] unknown,) does pollute [the] not yet born? With you sat [the one] by you condemned, and not did pollute you Felicianus? I him not have seen, you him have known; I him innocent believe, you this one guilty have condemned. Or if you confess of [an] innocent you to have been [the] receiver, you confess of [an] innocent you to have been [the] condemner.

bible_refs.note: Quoted: 'uenenum aspidum sub labiis eorum quorum os maledictione et amaritudine plenum est. ueloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem. contritio et infelicitas in uiis eorum, et uiam pacis non cognouerunt. non est timor dei ante oculos eorum.' Septuagint Psalm 13:3; Hebrew numbering Psalm 14:3.

pass_b_english: My brothers, every time we raised this case of the Maximianists against them in the conference—the case I have laid out for you as best I could—he was more silent about it then than he is now about everything. Let them not hide themselves with a quibbling not-defense but flight. For they say that they gave them a grace period and received them back within the grace period. This is false. Twelve men were condemned with Maximianus, but the rest were not present at his ordination when hands were laid on him. They gave those others a grace period. For these are his own words: 'And not only him,' he says, 'does a just death condemn for his crime; the chain of sacrilege drags very many others into partnership in the offense, of whom it is written: the poison of asps is under their lips, whose mouth is full of cursing and bitterness. Their feet are swift to shed blood. Ruin and misery are in their paths, and the way of peace they have not known. There is no fear of God before their eyes' (Psalm 13:3 LXX; cf. Romans 3:13-18). 'We would not wish, of course, to cut the joint as if it were our own body. But since the pestilential rottenness of a wasting wound has more relief in cutting off than in the application of medicine, a more wholesome course was found, so that the pestilent virus should not creep through all the limbs: that the wound, once formed, should fall away by brief pain.' So he names twelve men as guilty of a notorious crime, among them Felicianus and Praetextatus—though the names of all of them do not come to my mind—and then he concludes: 'Know that those who by the deadly work of destruction defiled a filthy vessel with gathered dregs, and also the clerics of the church of Carthage at one time, who by taking part in the crime offered pandering to an illicit incest, have been condemned by the judgment of the presiding God through the truth-speaking mouth of the universal council. But those whom the shoots of the sacrilegious one did not pollute as young plants—that is, those who drew back their own hands from Maximianus's head with the shame of a reverent faith—we have permitted to return to mother church.' They wanted to pumice their face, because they were pardoning sacrilegious men and openly granting schismatics a way to return. What is this, I ask? Let him now deign to explain to me how the shoots of the sacrilegious one did not pollute them as young plants. Why do you give them a grace period, if they could have had no part in Maximianus's schism? But if they are partners in the faction, even though they were not present at the ordination, how does Maximianus not defile them, while Caecilian—once condemned in his absence, and for the third time acquitted in his presence—defiles the whole world? An African does not defile Africans, a living man the living, a known man the known, a participant his partners—and Caecilian defiles those across the sea, defiles those far away, defiles the unknown, defiles those not yet born? Felicianus sat with you after being condemned by you, and he did not defile you? I never saw him; you knew him. I believe him innocent; you condemned him as guilty. Or if you admit that you received an innocent man, you admit that you condemned an innocent man.

problems.source_quote: de quibus scriptum est: (uenenum aspidum sub labiis eorum quorum os maledictione et amaritudine plenum est. ueloces pedes eorum ad effundendum sanguinem. contritio et infelicitas in uiis eorum, et uiam pacis non cognouerunt. non est timor dei ante oculos eorum
problems.why: The quotation is from Psalm 13:3 in the Vulgate/Hebrew numbering, but the Septuagint numbering would be Psalm 13:3 as well (Psalm 14:3 in Hebrew). However, the citation given as 'Psalm 13:3 (LXX)' is confusing because in the Septuagint this is Psalm 13, but the content matches Romans 3:13-18 which quotes multiple psalms. More importantly, the source marks this as scriptural quotation with 'de quibus scriptum est' but the English adds '(Psalm 13:3 (LXX))' which is incorrect—the passage is a composite quotation found in Romans 3:13-18, not a single Psalm 13:3. The LXX Psalm 13:3 only contains 'non est qui faciat bonum, non est usque ad unum.' The quoted material actually begins at what corresponds to Psalm 5:10 (LXX), Psalm 140:3 (LXX), etc. The citation is wrong.

problems.quote: how the shoots of the sacrilegious one did not pollute them as nurslings
problems.source_quote: quomodo eos sacrilegi surculi non polluere plantaria
problems.why: 'plantaria' means 'young plants, shoots, slips'—not 'nurslings' (which would be 'nutricii' or similar). 'Plantaria' is a botanical term matching 'surculi' (shoots). The English 'nurslings' introduces a human/animal metaphor not in the Latin. 'Plantaria' = 'young plants, seedlings.' The metaphor is consistently botanical: shoots polluting young plants.
problems.fix: how the shoots of the sacrilegious one did not pollute them as young plants
problems.ruling: 'plantaria' = young plants/seedlings; 'nurslings' is wrong, breaks botanical metaphor with 'surculi' (shoots).

problems.quote: once condemned in his absence, three times acquitted in his presence
problems.source_quote: semel absens damnatus, tertio praesens absolutus
problems.why: 'tertio' = 'three times' or 'for the third time.' The English 'three times acquitted in his presence' is ambiguous—does it mean 'on three occasions' or 'for a third time'? The Latin 'tertio praesens absolutus' means 'acquitted while present for the third time' (contrasted with 'semel absens damnatus' = 'once condemned in his absence'). The English 'three times' suggests multiple acquittals rather than 'for the third time' as a specific instance. This changes the rhetorical contrast: Augustine emphasizes Caecilian was condemned once absent but acquitted three times present—'tertio' is 'for the third time' (a specific enumeration), not merely 'three times.'
problems.fix: once condemned in his absence, and for the third time acquitted in his presence
problems.ruling: 'tertio' = 'for the third time' contrasting 'semel' = 'once'; 'three times' misreads specific enumeration as repeated count.

problems.why: The quotation is from Psalm 13:3 (LXX) / Psalm 14:3 (Hebrew), not Romans 3:13-18. While Paul quotes these verses in Romans, Augustine attributes them with 'de quibus scriptum est' to Scripture generally, and the source context points to Psalms as the primary citation.

fixed: The quotation is from Psalm 13:3 (LXX) / Psalm 14:3 (Hebrew), not Romans 3:13-18; the source says 'de quibus scriptum est' and the verses are Psalm 13:3 LXX, so the citation is corrected to Psalm 13:3 LXX with a cross-reference to Romans 3:13-18.

dismissed.why: The source quotes Psalm 13:3 LXX (Hebrew 14:3) but the citation should be Psalm 13:3 for 'venenum aspidum' only; the longer quotation from 'veloces pedes' onward is Psalm 13:7 LXX (Hebrew 14:7), not Romans 3:13-18. The English wrongly attributes the whole string to Psalm 13:3 LXX with Romans as cf.
dismissed.note: The whole chain stands in LXX Psalm 13:3, borrowed from Romans 3:13-18 and absent from Hebrew Psalm 14, so the citation is right and '13:7' is wrong.
